players.product: Mozaic HAMR nearline HDDs (44TB Mozaic 4+ -> 50TB Mozaic 5) for AI mass-capacity storage

quarterly_data.signal: TWO-LAYER ORDER BOOK: BUILD-TO-ORDER POs FOR 4-5 QUARTERS ON TOP OF 2-3 YEAR LTAs (CFO Gianluca Romano). 'We have purchase orders in place for the next 4 or 5 quarters, and that are very specific POs with the right mix, with the right price, with the right time to deliver', sitting on top of longer-term LTAs 'in place for the next 2, 3 years' where Seagate commits a certain exabyte volume so customers can plan data center growth - and those LTA volumes go up year over year. Seagate builds little flexibility into them ('we try to allocate all what we think we can produce') and says that at every renegotiation 'our customers are asking for more volume, not less volume'. On that basis management sees no digestion of deployed HDD capacity over the next two to three years.
quarterly_data.figure: POs in place for the next 4 or 5 quarters; LTAs in place for the next 2, 3 years with volumes rising year over year

quarterly_data.signal: CAPACITY ADDED WITHIN A 4%-6% CAPEX ENVELOPE - BUT HAMR HEADS NEED MORE CLEANROOM SPACE: a HAMR head wafer must run through all the existing PMR equipment and then through specific HAMR equipment, so cycle time is longer - 'if you want to extract the same volume, you need a little bit more space or you need to start more wafer and get the same output'. On the PMR side, capacity growth still comes from more heads and more media rather than technology. All of it fits inside Seagate's 4% and 6% of revenue CapEx range and yields 'the same number of units, but about 25% more exabyte'. Exabyte output will be lumpier across the 40-to-50 terabyte transition (line preparation quarters grow little, then output jumps), but the CAGR stays about 25%.
quarterly_data.figure: CapEx held at 4% and 6% of revenue; same number of units but about 25% more exabyte; at least 25% exabyte CAGR over the next two or three years

quarterly_data.signal: CAPACITY-PER-DRIVE NOW SPLITS BY CUSTOMER TYPE AS ON-PREM/ENTERPRISE OEM DEMAND RETURNS: 'Today, if we sell a 40 terabyte drive to a public cloud, we probably sell a 28, 30 terabyte drive to on-prem data center', because on-prem architectures are not yet built to absorb the largest drive - management expects on-prem to consume the 40 terabyte drive in about two years. Public cloud carried the first part of the last three years of demand growth; enterprise OEM / on-prem data center demand has since started to grow again and management expects it to become 'very important to this business', with some new AI applications likely to stay on-prem or hybrid.
quarterly_data.figure: public cloud buying 40 terabyte drives while on-prem buys 28, 30 terabyte; on-prem expected at 40 terabyte in about two years

quarterly_data.signal: TWO STRUCTURAL OPTION VALUES MANAGEMENT FLAGGED FOR HDD - KV CACHE TIERING AND NEOCLOUD-OWNED STORAGE. On KV cache: between cold storage (HDD) and the running application (NAND) sits a warm-storage tier with several sub-tiers, and 'for sure there are some tiers inside KV cache that can use hard disk drive' - the only place where NAND and HDD overlap. Seagate does not need a flash partner for it, only to meet the performance requirement of the relevant tier. On neoclouds: today they run compute against storage that physically sits in the public cloud, so Seagate sells the same drives to the same public-cloud customers; if neoclouds start serving their own customers they 'cannot access the public cloud storage anymore' and will need their own storage, shifting some of that volume directly to neoclouds - positive for customer diversification, roughly neutral on volume.
